messages.author: 55e546e375e22a40
messages.subject: summary.scanone
parts:
Hi,
I have run a genome-wide scanone on multiple phenotypes followed by 1000 permutations for LOD thresholds. Now I want to use summary.scanone() to get the adjusted pvalues and write to a table. Unfortunately, this is causing me some trouble. This is the command:
summary(output, format="allpheno", perms=output.perm, alpha=0.05, pvalues=TRUE)

This returns:

Length Class   Mode
[1,] 3      scanone list
[2,] 3      scanone list
.......nphe(class)

to write table, I use:

Is there a way to get the summary.scanone() to work for all the phenotypes?

Thanks.

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] summary.scanone
parts:
There's something wrong with the format of the 'output' object. It doesn't seem to be straight scanone output.

It may be a list of scanone objects, in which case you can combine them into one object through the following:

for(i in 2:length(output)) output[[1]] <- cbind(output[[1]], output[[i]])
output <- output[[1]]

For summary.scanone with multiple LOD curves, I prefer format="tabByChr" and format="tabByCol"; you might try those.

karl

parts:
The simplest thing is to just use colnames(). For example:

colnames(output) <- c("chr", "pos", phenames(mycross))

or

colnames(output)[-(1:2)] <- phenames(mycross)

karl

messages.author: 04e62c3b36bb17bf
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] summary.scanone
parts:
Hi all. I recently found this post very useful and figured I would add a point here. 
When doing eQTL analysis, you may find that you need to cbind a very large list of scanone objects. For example, R/qtlhot needs a large multi-phenotype scanone object. If you generated scanones using multiple QTL modeling, you would then need to make a single scanone out of many.
Karl's solution below works well for <5000 phenotypes; however, for more phenotypes, it becomes very slow. The work around posted below splits up the task into chucks of scanone objects (default is 100), then binds those objects back together.  This takes <2minutes for 10000 traits, whereas the single scanone approach takes several hours on my machine. 
Cheers,
John

Here is the function:

combine.s1<-function(s1s,n=100){
  sets<-split(1:length(s1s), ceiling(seq_along(1:length(s1s))/n))
  cat("combining scanones by sets of", n, " ")
  out.byset<-list()
  for(i in 1:length(sets)){
    out.byset[[i]]<-s1.test[[sets[[i]][1]]]
    for(j in (min(sets[[i]])+1): max(sets[[i]])){
      out.byset[[i]]<-cbind(out.byset[[i]], s1.test[[j]])
    }
    cat(length(out.byset)*n,"...")
  }
  out.all<-out.byset[[1]]
  cat(" combining sets (total =",length(s1s),") : ")
  for(i in 2:length(out.byset))  {
    out.all<-cbind(out.all, out.byset[[i]])
    cat(length(colnames(out.all)),"...")
  }
  return(out.all)
}

#not run
cbinded.scanones<-combine.s1(list.of.scanones)

  output <- output[[1]]

For summary.scanone with multiple LOD curves, I prefer format="tabByChr" and format="tabByCol"; you might try those.

karl
